before.value: Treat the complaint as the initial report, the incident as the actual event being described, and the case or FIR as the formal police record once it is accepted for action. Suspect, accused, witness, and victim should be separate role labels tied to a person within that case, and the same person may carry more than one role at different stages. If there is ambiguity, keep the record provisional until an authorized officer confirms the correct classification rather than forcing a wrong label early.

after.value: Treat the complaint as the initial report and allow the receiving officer to classify it based on the nature and seriousness of the report. A minor information-only entry can stay as a complaint or incident, while a cognizable matter can be opened as a formal case or FIR. If more facts come in later and the status changes, the record should be reclassified without losing the original submission history, so it remains clear what was reported first and why the category changed. If the same person's role shifts, such as from complainant to witness or suspect, the system should preserve the earlier role in the audit trail and show the current role clearly going forward.

before.value: Keep the original record when a complaint moves between stations or higher authority, record where it was transferred, when, and to whom so the trail is not lost, and keep an audit trail of every change. Records staff should maintain the official complaint entry, ensure basic details are complete and standardized, correct obvious data issues, manage references, filing numbers, transfers, and the linkage between the complaint and the investigation record, and validate/preserve the proper version when official corrections to names or jurisdiction occur. In practice, the old paper or legacy record is first registered in the new system with a unique reference, the core details are verified (complainant name, date, location, current status), and records staff track what has been transferred while keeping the official master entry. During any short parallel period, updates must be entered into both systems or reconciled by records staff the same day so the versions do not drift apart; after cutover, one clearly designated source of truth must be used and any changes synchronized under that rule. If a case has been transferred or taken over by a higher office, the current controlling office should be the primary jurisdiction shown, but the original station or district name should still be kept in the history.

before.value: The system should keep an audit trail of every change, including case record creation or updates, investigation notes, evidence links, person links, status changes, routing to another unit, and recorded follow-up actions. Temporary access for sensitive victim, witness, suspect, or evidence information should be granted deliberately and logged, with automatic expiry unless renewed for a valid reason. Records staff should maintain the official complaint entry, correct obvious data issues, manage references, filing numbers, transfers, and the linkage between the complaint and the investigation record, and validate and preserve the proper version when official corrections such as names or jurisdiction changes occur. The system should also allow the record to remain provisional when complaint, incident, and person-role classifications are ambiguous until an authorized officer confirms the correct classification. Renewals of temporary access should be recorded with a reason so there is an audit trail. During any parallel cutover period, any update made in one place should be entered into the other as well, or reconciled by records staff the same day, and after cutover changes should be logged and synchronized under a single designated source of truth so the two versions do not drift apart. Citizens may submit additional details or documents against the same complaint number through their own account or a secure link tied to the complaint, but they cannot alter the official record themselves once the complaint is in progress; only their additions or clarifications go to police review. If more facts come in later and the status changes, the record should be reclassified without losing the original submission history, so we can see what was reported first and why the category changed. If the same person’s role shifts, such as from complainant to witness or even suspect, the system should preserve the earlier role in the audit trail and show the current role clearly going forward.

before.value: Once a matter moves to transfer, court, or closure, edit rights should narrow based on role and responsibility, so only the currently assigned unit and authorized supervisors can change the active record. Sensitive details should remain viewable only to staff with a need to know, while citizens should usually see only the status and whatever notices are meant for them. Actions like reopening, changing ownership, or editing finalized notes should be blocked unless there is an exceptional override for a clerical error, new evidence, a court return, or a supervisory review that finds the case was closed too early. Ordinary users should not be able to do it; it should require approval from a supervisor or a higher-ranking officer, and in some cases both the originating and receiving unit may need to confirm it. Any such override should be logged with the reason, approver, and timestamp so there is a clear audit trail.

before.value: Keep the original record when a complaint moves between stations or higher authority, record where it was transferred, when, and to whom so the trail is not lost, and keep an audit trail of every change. Records staff should maintain the official complaint entry, ensure basic details are complete and standardized, correct obvious data issues, manage references, filing numbers, transfers, and the linkage between the complaint and the investigation record, and validate/preserve the proper version when official corrections to names or jurisdiction occur. In practice, the old paper or legacy record is first registered in the new system with a unique reference, the core details are verified (complainant name, date, location, current status), and records staff track what has been transferred while keeping the official master entry. During any short parallel period, updates must be entered into both systems or reconciled by records staff the same day so the versions do not drift apart; after cutover, one clearly designated source of truth must be used and any changes synchronized under that rule. If a case has been transferred or taken over by a higher office, the current controlling office should be the primary jurisdiction shown, but the original station or district name should still be kept in the history. Overrides to reopen a case, change ownership, or edit finalized notes should be allowed only in exceptional situations such as a clerical error, new evidence, a court return, or a supervisory review finding the case was closed too early, and must be approved by a supervisor or higher-ranking officer; in some cases both the originating and receiving unit may need to confirm. Any such override should be logged with the reason, approver, and timestamp so there is a clear audit trail.

before.value: Exact retention periods must come from the ministry’s records schedule and legal guidance. Updated records should keep the prior version in an audit history. Duplicated records should carry a source reference. Anything shared with another system should preserve the original retention status. Deletion or redaction should only happen when the retention period has expired or when there is a legal requirement to protect personal data, and a minimal audit record should be kept to show the action occurred. When a receiving unit needs to redact or restrict part of shared information for privacy or operational reasons, it may create a restricted view or redacted copy for operational use, but the original record must remain intact in the source case file, with the underlying evidence and audit history unchanged. The system must track what was redacted, who did it, when it was done, and why, while keeping the original retention rules tied to the master record.

before.value: When records are shared between police units during an active investigation, the receiving unit may create a restricted view or redacted copy for operational use, but the original record must remain intact in the source case file. The system should record what was redacted, who did it, when it was done, and why, while keeping the original retention rules tied to the master record. Further hiding by the receiving unit must only affect that unit's users and must not alter the underlying evidence or audit history. Exception handling should exist for urgent operational situations, with only authorized supervisors or designated officers able to approve access to redacted or sensitive records. Any bypass of normal controls should trigger escalation and a mandatory after-the-fact review. If audit logging cannot be fully captured in the moment, the system should require a manual incident note and late entry of the reason, approver, and affected records as soon as possible. It should also support audit logging so we can see who viewed or changed what.

before.value: If a dependent system is unavailable or the approving office is closed, the request should stay pending with a clear reason and timestamp rather than being dropped; urgent matters should use a fallback manual process so the officer can continue and complete the formal step later, while non-urgent items can wait in a queue and be routed automatically once service resumes. Pending items should remain visible in a suspended or pending state so staff can see they are not lost, with the reason for the delay recorded. If the dependency is unavailable only briefly, items can wait in queue; if the outage exceeds an operational threshold, a manual workaround is allowed only for urgent cases and with supervisor awareness. Once the other system or office is back, the items should resume from where they stopped, and the system should track what was completed manually so nothing gets duplicated. Exceptional overrides after transfer, court send, or closure are allowed only for clerical error, new evidence, court return, or supervisory review showing the case was closed too early; ordinary users cannot do this, approval must come from a supervisor or higher-ranking officer, and in some cases both the originating and receiving unit must confirm. All overrides must be logged with reason, approver, and timestamp for audit trail.

before.value: Must follow internal police and ministry SOPs for access control, audit logging, and case file preservation, with exception handling allowed for urgent operational situations. Only authorized supervisors or designated officers may approve access to redacted or sensitive records. Temporary access renewal should be approved when the investigation is still active, the officer still has a legitimate need to know, and the original access period is about to expire before the work is complete; it also covers court preparation, follow-up witness checks, and pending forensic review where access is still necessary. Renewal authorization would be by the case supervisor or unit head depending on sensitivity, but the exact approval ladder should be confirmed with the ministry. Any bypass of normal controls should trigger escalation and a mandatory after-the-fact review. If audit logging cannot be fully captured in the moment, a manual incident note and late entry of the reason, approver, and affected records must be completed as soon as possible. In the first release, only a small set of trusted administrators should be able to create, edit, disable, or assign roles to users, and those actions should be logged. Changes in access when someone moves to another station or needs access to a different case should require approval by the local supervisor or records lead rather than happening automatically. Cross-station access should be kept very limited, exposing only what people need for their work. Trusted administrators should be blocked from changing their own critical access, and any action affecting superuser accounts, audit-only accounts, or users in another station should require a second approval or separate admin process. Disabling the last active administrator in a unit should not be allowed without oversight.

before.value: Keep an audit trail of every change and treat evidence as chain-of-custody material with clear time and officer records, especially when evidence is attached, shared between units, or handed over to court. Only authorized officers and records staff should be able to handle evidence, and every attachment or handoff should log the officer’s identity, date and time, unit, and what was transferred. If evidence moves between units, the system should keep a clear chain-of-custody trail so we can see who had it at each step and when. Updated records should keep the prior version in an audit history; duplicated records should carry a source reference; anything shared with another system should preserve the original retention status. Deletion or redaction should only happen when the retention period has expired or when there is a legal requirement to protect personal data, and even then a minimal audit record of the action should be kept. The receiving unit may create a restricted view or redacted copy for operational use, but the original record must remain intact in the source case file; the system must track what was redacted, who did it, when it was done, and why, while keeping the original retention rules tied to the master record. Further hiding by the receiving unit must not change the underlying evidence or audit history, only the visibility for that unit’s users. If audit logging cannot be fully captured in the moment, the system should require a manual incident note and late entry of the reason, approver, and affected records as soon as possible. Only authorized investigation or records staff should be able to add or replace documents, and the system must keep a clear audit trail of who did what and when. Viewing should be based on role and case access, with sensitive or evidentiary files restricted to people directly involved in the matter. Once a case has been shared, transferred, or moved forward, removing or replacing evidence-related files should be tightly controlled and usually require approval, because we need to preserve the integrity of the record.

before.value: When records are shared between police units during an active investigation, the receiving unit may create a restricted view or redacted copy for operational use, but the original record must remain intact in the source case file. The system should record what was redacted, who did it, when it was done, and why, while keeping the original retention rules tied to the master record. Further hiding by the receiving unit must only affect that unit's users and must not alter the underlying evidence or audit history. Exception handling should exist for urgent operational situations, with only authorized supervisors or designated officers able to approve access to redacted or sensitive records. Any bypass of normal controls should trigger escalation and a mandatory after-the-fact review. If audit logging cannot be fully captured in the moment, the system should require a manual incident note and late entry of the reason, approver, and affected records as soon as possible. It should also support audit logging so we can see who viewed or changed what. For restricted actions, formal approval from the station or district authority is needed, along with a role-based permission update and a clear audit trail explaining why the exception was granted.

before.value: Restrict who can view or edit sensitive information to the assigned investigating officer, their supervising officer, and specifically authorized records staff; temporary access may be granted deliberately and logged for court requests, inter-unit transfers, or a backup officer covering the case, and that access should expire automatically unless renewed for a valid reason. Extensions should only be granted when the officer still needs the information for an active investigation, a legal proceeding, or a formally assigned follow-up task, and approval should come from the supervising officer or another clearly designated authorized manager, not the user themselves. Access should be restricted when the material is sensitive, part of an open investigation, involves a juvenile or victim privacy, or is legally sealed, and in those cases only approved users should be able to view it. In urgent operational situations, exceptions may be allowed, but only authorized supervisors or designated officers may approve access to redacted or sensitive records, and any bypass of normal controls must trigger escalation and a mandatory after-the-fact review. Temporary access renewal should be approved when the investigation is still active, the officer still has a legitimate need to know, and the original access period is about to expire before the work is complete; it should also cover court preparation, follow-up witness checks, or pending forensic review. Renewal authorization should come from the case supervisor or unit head, depending on the sensitivity level, with the exact approval ladder to be confirmed with the ministry. If someone moves to another station or needs access to a different case, that change should go through approval by the local supervisor or records lead rather than being automatic. Cross-station access should stay very limited so people only see what they need for their work.

after.value: The audit log should be protected so only authorized supervisory or audit users can view it; for sensitive or sealed cases it should be even more restricted, but it should not be deleted or hidden from oversight users.

before.value: When records are shared between police units during an active investigation, the receiving unit may create a restricted view or redacted copy for operational use, but the original record must remain intact in the source case file. The system should record what was redacted, who did it, when it was done, and why, while keeping the original retention rules tied to the master record. Further hiding by the receiving unit must only affect that unit's users and must not alter the underlying evidence or audit history. Exception handling should exist for urgent operational situations, with only authorized supervisors or designated officers able to approve access to redacted or sensitive records. Any bypass of normal controls should trigger escalation and a mandatory after-the-fact review. If audit logging cannot be fully captured in the moment, the system should require a manual incident note and late entry of the reason, approver, and affected records as soon as possible. It should also support audit logging so we can see who viewed or changed what. For restricted actions, formal approval from the station or district authority is needed, along with a role-based permission update and a clear audit trail explaining why the exception was granted.

Cross-station access should be kept very limited, exposing only what people need for their work. before.value: Keep the original record when a complaint moves between stations or higher authority, record where it was transferred, when, and to whom so the trail is not lost, and keep an audit trail of every change. Records staff should maintain the official complaint entry, ensure basic details are complete and standardized, correct obvious data issues, manage references, filing numbers, transfers, and the linkage between the complaint and the investigation record, and validate/preserve the proper version when official corrections to names or jurisdiction occur. In practice, the old paper or legacy record is first registered in the new system with a unique reference, the core details are verified (complainant name, date, location, current status), and records staff track what has been transferred while keeping the official master entry. During any short parallel period, updates must be entered into both systems or reconciled by records staff the same day so the versions do not drift apart; after cutover, one clearly designated source of truth must be used and any changes synchronized under that rule. If a case has been transferred or taken over by a higher office, the current controlling office should be the primary jurisdiction shown, but the original station or district name should still be kept in the history. Overrides to reopen a case, change ownership, or edit finalized notes should be allowed only in exceptional situations such as a clerical error, new evidence, a court return, or a supervisory review finding the case was closed too early, and must be approved by a supervisor or higher-ranking officer; in some cases both the originating and receiving unit may need to confirm. Any such override should be logged with the reason, approver, and timestamp so there is a clear audit trail. The initial foundation release should also include audit logging so it is possible to see who viewed or changed what.

before.value: Keep an audit trail of every change so it is visible who viewed or changed what; only authorized investigation or records staff should be able to add or replace FIRs, statements, and evidence references. Viewing should be based on role and case access, with sensitive or evidentiary files restricted to people directly involved in the matter. Once a case has been shared, transferred, or moved forward, removing or replacing evidence-related files should be tightly controlled and usually require approval to preserve the integrity of the record. An audit trail is needed from the start to keep the system accountable. Sensitive details like witness identities, informant data, and restricted evidence should only be visible to users with the right role and clearance, and in some cases only a redacted summary should be shared. Only a very small set of users should see sensitive or sealed-case manual escalation logs, mainly the assigned supervisor, a designated internal auditor, and perhaps a higher-ranking oversight authority if the case is formally sealed or under special review. Supervisors should only access it for legitimate operational reasons, auditors should access it for compliance or investigation purposes, and both accesses should be logged themselves. If a case is sealed, even those users should see the minimum necessary detail, with the most sensitive content masked unless there is explicit authorization.
